Before getting into landslides I want to cover what a stereonet is.

A stereonet is a type of stereographic projection. Basically it's what you get if you take a hemisphere and flattened it out on a 2d sheet of paper. So imagine a clear cereal bowl with lines drawn on it marking different degrees. If you shine a powerful light on it from directly above a stereonet is the shadow that is left by it. The outer edge of the circle is the 0Â° mark (horizontal angle), while the center of the circle is 90Â° (straight up and down, or orthogonal). The outer edge is usually marked in 0Â° - 360Â° increments that correspond to compass directions. Most geologists use some type of Brunton field compass to measure the orientation of bedding planes, joints, or any other planar structures in rocks in 3D space. A stereonet is used to plot these 3D features onto a 2D sheet of paper.

If you were to take the clear cereal bowl and cut out a sheet of paper to perfectly fit the inside of the hemisphere, you could insert the paper into the bowl at any angle. The places where the paper touch the inside of the bowl will make a curved line when plotted onto the stereonet. The curved line is the contact of a planar surface with the inside of a hemisphere. It looks like these lines. Here is another picture showing planes on the inside of a sphere.

With landslides we are interested with planes of weakness.

One type of plane of weakness is bedding planes. When sediment is deposited, it usually is deposited in flat lying layers (this is an oversimplification, but it's the rule of thumb). When you see sedimentary rocks, you can often see straight lines in the rock where things suddenly change. This is especially true of shale. Shale is a sedimentary rock made of mud that gets deposited, buried, and then lithifies under pressure. Once the pressure is removed it likes to foliate, breaking into separate flat brittle sheets. If you put orthogonal pressure onto this rock (pushing straight down on it), it is strong. If the pressure is coming from any other angle though the rock is weak. Shale layers in sedimentary rocks often act like astroglide between other layers of rock. It allows the rocks to move past each other very easily.

The other major plane of weakness is called a joint. Since rock is solid on human time scales it has a crystal lattice. Joints are breaks that occur along that lattice. A good example of this is limestone, since it joints at 90Â° angles. Here is jointed limestone and here is unjointed limestone. The second image does have joint faces pointing towards the camera, so it's technically still jointed, but there are not joints in the body of the rock.

These planes can be measured with a Brunton compass, where their strike (orientation of a horizontal line on the plane with respect to cardinal directions), dip (the angle of the plane related to up and down), and dip direction (the cardinal direction that the plane is dipping towards - always 90Â° from strike). Think of a boat ramp. It dips into the water. The strike is the water line on the ramp. The dip is the angle of the boat ramp. The dip direction is the direction on the surface of the water that the dip is dipping in. With those three numbers, you can plot a plane on a stereonet.
